title: AI scams in Georgia and South Florida: How scammers use deepfakes to steal millions

reading.body:
This is impersonation, not malfunction. The systems involved are generative tools used to clone a voice, fabricate a photograph, or spoof a caller ID, and they are pointed at people rather than at institutions. The output is consumed directly by the target, who hears a relative or a named immigration attorney and has no second channel in which to check. Nothing in the reporting describes a deployed product failing its own specifications. It describes synthetic media being used as the opening move of a fraud.

The vulnerable point is the first contact, a phone call or a social media message that arrives already looking and sounding legitimate. Because the impersonation is of a specific real person, the usual signals of a scam, a wrong name, a clumsy accent, an unfamiliar account, are absent by design. Catching it would have required the target to verify through a channel they initiated themselves, or a prearranged code word, or a pause before acting on urgency. Those are the defenses the reporting says banks and authorities recommend, which places the check on the recipient rather than anywhere in the pipeline that produced the fake.

What is not established is who built or supplied the tools, which platforms carried the messages, or whether any of them detected the activity. The loss figures come from reported complaints, which are allegations of harm rather than adjudicated findings, and the cloning of the attorney's identity rests on his account and the outlets' reporting. No court has ruled on these cases in the material given.

summary:
Criminals are increasingly using artificial intelligence to commit scams across Georgia and South Florida by creating deepfakes of voices, photos, and phone calls that sound and look authentic. Recent cases include a South Florida immigration attorney whose voice and identity were cloned to target vulnerable immigrants, and a Cobb County couple who lost approximately $800,000 in a cryptocurrency scam. According to the FBI's 2025 Internet Crime Report, Americans reported nearly $893 million in AI-enabled scam losses last year, with Florida accounting for 350 complaints totaling $39.9 million and Georgia reporting 71 complaints totaling $10.4 million in losses.

Scammers are using AI to enhance traditional fraud schemes by cloning voices from social media, spoofing legitimate phone numbers, creating fake photographs, and researching personal relationships to make emergency requests more convincing. One common variation is the AI grandparent scam, where criminals mimic a relative's voice to claim the grandchild needs urgent money. Banks warn customers to verify urgent requests through trusted channels, pause before responding to unexpected communications, and monitor account activity closely. Authorities recommend families establish secret code words to verify identities and emphasize that verification rather than speed offers the strongest defense against these evolving scams.
